concept.name: Interest rate future
concept.definition: A standardized, exchange-traded futures contract whose underlying is an interest rate or an interest-bearing instrument — such as U.S. Treasury, SOFR, or Fed Funds futures — used to hedge or express views on interest rates at maturities from one week to 30 years.
concept.intuition: An interest rate future lets you lock in or bet on where rates will be months or years from now, in a standardized, centrally cleared contract.
concept.mechanics: Contracts are margined and marked to market daily with central clearing. Short-term interest rate (STIR) futures are quoted on an index basis as 100 minus the implied forward rate; Treasury futures are settled by delivery of eligible bonds or notes, with exchange-published conversion factors making a range of maturities deliverable and creating a cheapest-to-deliver.
concept.formula: STIR futures price (IMM index convention) = 100 - implied forward rate. Treasury futures invoice price = contract size x futures settlement price x conversion factor + accrued interest.
concept.failure_modes: STIR futures carry a convexity bias relative to FRAs and swaps, so naive rate readings are off. Treasury futures hedges face basis and cheapest-to-deliver shifts, and daily marking generates margin calls in fast-moving rate markets.
concept.misconceptions: That a rising STIR futures price means rising rates — under the 100-minus-rate convention it means the opposite. Also, buying a Treasury future is not buying a specific bond; the short chooses which eligible bond to deliver.
concept.example: A pension manager sells 10-year Treasury futures to shorten portfolio duration ahead of an expected rate rise, offsetting losses on its cash bond holdings.
